vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: openclaw-usage-dashboard
Version: 2.0.1

The skill bundle provides a local usage dashboard but contains high-risk behaviors and a potential security vulnerability. In `server.js`, the script uses `child_process.execSync` to execute system commands for health monitoring and to automatically open the browser. A shell injection vulnerability exists because the `HOST` and `PORT` command-line arguments are interpolated directly into an `execSync` call without sanitization. Furthermore, the skill requires broad read access to the user's home directory (`~/.openclaw`) to parse session logs and configuration files. While the implementation includes defensive features like secret redaction regexes and a strict Content Security Policy, the combination of shell execution and sensitive file access meets the threshold for a suspicious classification.

llm.summary: The skill's code and instructions match its stated purpose (a local, read-only dashboard for OpenClaw session logs); nothing in the package requests unrelated credentials or appears to exfiltrate data, though you should still review and trust the unknown source before running it locally.

dimensions.detail: Name/description (local dashboard for OpenClaw usage) aligns with the included files: server.js and dashboard.html implement a localhost web UI that parses ~/.openclaw/agents/*/sessions/*.jsonl. Minor inconsistency: the registry metadata lists 'Required config paths: none' while SKILL.md and server.js explicitly read the OpenClaw session path in the user's home directory—this should have been declared but is proportional to the stated purpose.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md tells the agent to run `node server.js` and open localhost. server.js reads local session logs, aggregates metrics, and serves the dashboard on localhost. The code uses child_process.execSync for local system-health commands (vm_stat, df, powershell, openclaw version, open/xdg-open); the audit and code comments state no user input is interpolated into shell commands. No instructions or code paths indicate transmission of data to external services.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec or external downloads — instruction-only with bundled source files. No packages are fetched at install time and there is no remote install URL, so nothing arbitrary is pulled from the network during install.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires no environment variables or credentials. It does read files under the user's home (~/.openclaw/agents/...), which is appropriate for a usage dashboard. The manifest's omission of the required config path is a minor coherence gap. The code contains secret-redaction patterns and a whitelist of risky fields to avoid exposing raw secrets, but reading session logs inherently accesses potentially sensitive local data — that's expected for this tool but worth noting.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Flags are default (always: false, user-invocable). The skill does not request persistent platform privileges or modify other skills. It runs as a local process only when invoked by the user/agent.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This package appears to do exactly what it says: run a Node server that parses local OpenClaw session logs and serves a dashboard on localhost. Things to consider before running: 1) Source trust — the package author and homepage are unknown; review server.js and dashboard.html yourself or run in a restricted environment. 2) Local data access — the server reads ~/.openclaw/agents/*/sessions/*.jsonl; these logs may contain sensitive content even if the code tries to redact patterns. 3) child_process usage — server.js runs fixed system commands for health info (no user input interpolation is claimed), but confirm there is no unexpected shell invocation in the full file. 4) Performance — the server uses synchronous file IO and has limits (MAX_SESSIONS, MEMORY_BUDGET_MB); expect blocking behaviour for very large logs. If you don't want to run it directly, inspect the two code files for any network calls (none were found in the provided snippets) or run it inside a sandbox/container with restricted network access.
